draft: This noun does one of the oldest jobs in English: it points to the person enrolled in schooling, from the first primer to the highest degree. Its root sits not in the schoolroom but in keenness, in pressing on, in holding to one subject with effort. Present use stretches wide: children in reception rooms, working folk in evening courses, PhD hopefuls in their thirties. Editors quibble over two points. Some hold the term should end when the enrolment ends; others let it cover self-schooled folk who never enrol. Both senses persist in print, so context, not the noun itself, decides which one is intended.

scenario.task: Write a short piece for a language column on the word student: its history, its current sense, and the reason editors argue about it.

draft: This tiny hedge carries three different senses by turns: mere, exactly, and very recently. In a first draft it nearly always arrives as the padding beat a writer inserts while thinking. It shrinks whatever trails it: a quick change, a minute later, a tiny tweak. That shrinking is the risk. Tell a client the fix is that easy, then bill a week, and the reader will feel misled. The test is easy: strike it and read the line again. If the meaning is the same, leave it stricken; if the line breaks, it was earning its keep. Kept deliberately, it is a real intensifier; kept by habit, it is filler.

scenario.task: Write a 120-word entry for an in-house style guide explaining what the word just actually means to a reader, why writers reach for it, and what it does to a sentence.

draft: You reach for that vague catch-all term when you cannot yet name the real material. It can fill any gap, in any draft, at any hour. That width can comfort a writer, and it can betray them: a reader will meet the term and picture nothing at all. In live copy it will more often hide an item you could count: the equipment a crew hauled in, the paperwork the client owed, the extra work nobody quantified, the clutter in the cupboard. Try the exchange in edit: name the actual item, count it, price it. A named item can be checked, argued with, or denied. The vague term can be none of that.

scenario.task: Explain to a room of new copywriters why the word stuff keeps turning up in first drafts, and what it usually stands in for.

draft: The formal opener came out of legal and clerical writing, where the writer wanted a claim on the record without owning it. It travelled into academic writing by the identical route: an aloof alert, put in front of a fact the author wanted the reader to weigh. A modern editor will delete it nearly every time, and the remainder will read quicker and warmer. Nothing went with it that the reader ever wanted. In warm, direct copy - a note to a friend, a welcome letter, a thank-you card - the formal alert will land like a clipboard in a kitchen.

scenario.task: A dictionary editor has asked for a short entry describing the phrase it should be noted: where it came from, how it is handled today, and one sentence on the writing where it feels out of place.

attack.topic_span: the phrase it should be noted

draft: This four-word concessive tag is a participial absolute, cousin to having said that and to the older that said. It signals a turn: the writer concedes the previous point, then pivots against it. Readers hear it as a courtesy, a small bow before the disagreement arrives. The trouble is its weight. Four words of throat-clearing do the work one word does better; but, still and yet all pivot faster and sound less pleased with themselves. Keep the tag when the concession is real and the pivot genuinely matters, as in a review that praises a machine before condemning its price. Cut it when the pivot is small, and let the plain conjunction carry the turn.

scenario.task: Write a 120-word entry for an in-house style guide explaining what the phrase that being said actually means to a reader, why writers reach for it, and what it does to a sentence.

draft: This opener is the newest member of an old family, descended from nowadays and from in these times, both of which once sounded equally fresh. It claims currency: what follows is meant to be read as new, urgent, particular to the present moment. Its trouble is that the present tense already says so. A sentence about how people read now is about now, and the opener adds four words and no information. Editors also hear it as a signal of a coming platitude, because it so often introduces one. Keep it when the contrast with an earlier era is the actual point being made. Otherwise strike it and start with the noun that matters.

scenario.task: Write a short piece for a language column on the phrase in today's world: its history, its current sense, and the reason editors argue about it.

draft: The term began life as a Germanic name linked with the beech tree, since the earliest tablets were cut in beech. In present English it names nearly any bundle within a binding, at any length, in any language. These days it stretches past paper entirely: a reader with a tablet, a listener with earbuds at the wheel, a child with a bedtime tale in an app. It still hints at limits - a beginning, an end, a spine, a price - which is why it jars when a file is licensed by the year, altered by the publisher after release, and never really held. In print the term named a length; at present it names an intent.

scenario.task: A dictionary editor has asked for a short entry describing the word books: where it came from, how it is handled today, and one sentence on the writing where it feels out of place.

draft: The noun names the person on the receiving side of care: examined, treated, discharged, billed. Writers reach for it because it is short and because the whole system already uses it, from the ward whiteboard to the insurance claim. What it does to a sentence is quietly grammatical - it makes a human being the object. Things are done to them; they rarely act. That is why hospitals now write the person having surgery, or use the name, in anything a family will read. Keep the clinical noun for clinical writing, where the role really is the point. In a letter home, use the human being instead.

scenario.task: Write a 120-word entry for an in-house style guide explaining what the word patient actually means to a reader, why writers reach for it, and what it does to a sentence.

draft: The plural noun names a profession, but in most sentences it is doing something looser: standing in for medicine itself, or for expert authority in general. Writers reach for it because it is a fast, familiar shorthand - four in five recommend it, ask your physician, the professionals agree. That looseness is the danger. The plural implies consensus without naming who agreed, how many were asked, or in which field they trained. A cardiologist and a dermatologist are not interchangeable authorities. In careful copy, name the specialty, name the body that issued the guidance, or say clinicians and mean it. Save the plural for sentences where the profession as a whole really is the subject.

scenario.task: Write a 120-word entry for an in-house style guide explaining what the word doctors actually means to a reader, why writers reach for it, and what it does to a sentence.

draft: It turns up in first drafts because it is the shortest word for a large idea, and because clients say it in meetings. Nine times in ten it is standing in for something more exact that the writer has not yet pinned down. Sometimes it means the image itself. Sometimes it means the file, with its size and format and licence. Sometimes it means the shoot: half a day, a crew, a stylist, an invoice. Sometimes it means the evidence, as in proof that the work was done. Ask which one you mean, then write that instead. The rewritten line usually gets shorter, and the client stops asking what is included.

scenario.task: Explain to a room of new copywriters why the word photo keeps turning up in first drafts, and what it usually stands in for.

draft: Readers meet the term and picture a sunlit hillside, a family name at the gate, a life lived in gentle rhythm. The truth underneath is a farm: early starts, spray timetables, trellis wire, mildew, weeks with wet feet, thin margins, and a single freeze in April that can erase the entire year. Nearly every hillside estate is a small business with agricultural risk and delayed pay. Is the imagined picture fair? Partly. The image sells the drink, and the yearly rhythm really is gentler than a supermarket dairy line. The graft behind it deserves the same billing.

scenario.task: Draft a 100-word paragraph for a plain-language guide about the word vineyards, covering what readers assume when they meet it and whether that assumption is fair.

draft: The term rode into English from southern Europe, where it signified milk, nothing more. In English it now points to milk poured over one shot of the strong, bitter brew, in something like six to one. The drink itself grew common in the eighties; the term followed it onto every high street by the nineties. Editors bicker over just one point: whether to print it in the tilted type we give incomers, or to let it sit upright, English enough by now. The upright side is winning, since English long since swept the term into its own set, endings included. Its second life, in cheerful terms like the lunch-money index, tells us the term now points well beyond the drink.

scenario.task: Write a short piece for a language column on the word latte: its history, its current sense, and the reason editors argue about it.

draft: The noun arrived in English from Italian in the early twentieth century, where it named a drink made to order and made fast - the same root that gives us express. It names both a method and a measure: hot water forced under pressure through finely ground beans, and the small dark result, roughly thirty millilitres. Modern usage has stretched it. It now modifies half the drinks menu, so that a shot, a machine, a bar and a martini all borrow it, and it has become a marker of seriousness rather than a description of a process. It reads oddly in cooking copy, where the writer means only strong and dark, and the pressure that defines the word never appears.

scenario.task: A dictionary editor has asked for a short entry describing the word espresso: where it came from, how it is handled today, and one sentence on the writing where it feels out of place.

draft: The term came from medicine. In Latin it meant take, the imperative a medic wrote at the head of a mixture, and the apothecary read it that way until quite recently. By the eighteenth century the kitchen had taken the term over, and the medical remnant retreated into the chemical trade. Today it can name a printed method in a card tin, a video, a family memory nobody ever wrote down, or a metaphor: a method for calm, a method for ruin. In market copy the metaphor can dominate, where it will decorate any claim while adding nothing at all. Where the term truly fit, it worked like a fair deal: do the numbered work in the numbered order, and the outcome will repeat.

scenario.task: Write a short piece for a language column on the word recipes: its history, its current sense, and the reason editors argue about it.

draft: Two very different senses hide in this one term. One is the single written symbol; twenty-six such tokens hold the whole tongue. The other is the missive: folded sheets, the envelope, the postbox, the wet ink of someone missing you. Both descend from one root, which is why English keeps them under one roof. Do the two confuse people? Very seldom. Context settles it: the printer's sense sits next to type, size, weight, spelling, while the other sits next to sending, receiving, opening, replying. The flip between the two is honest, not sloppy, so the guess folk bring to this term is mostly sound, blessed by centuries of use.

scenario.task: Draft a 100-word paragraph for a plain-language guide about the word letter, covering what readers assume when they meet it and whether that assumption is fair.

draft: This tiny word will show up in first drafts of almost any product copy about calm, comfort, or output. It is a warm, dinky, comic word: no adult will admit to lying flat at midday, but all of us want to. So it stands in for grown-up nouns a copy pro will not put in a draft: a lull, a stop, an unpaid hour, a hint of burnout. In brand copy it also masks a claim with no clinical trial and no data at all, just a cosy word doing all of that work. Ask what it is doing in your own draft. If your claim is about a slump at half past two, put a fact in front of it: an hour off, and by 4pm your staff typos drop by a third.

scenario.task: Explain to a room of new copywriters why the word naps keeps turning up in first drafts, and what it usually stands in for.

draft: This noun holds two different senses under one term: enrolment in some course of study, plus, by implicit hint, youth or dependence. Writers pick it since it is short, since it is polite, plus it covers every discipline in one term. Its cost is subtle: it puts one hundred wildly different people into one single cohort, which lets the sentence get by without telling us who is in the room, or how old, or in which subject. Prefer the precise role where you know it: intern, recruit, first-term medic, evening enrolee. Reserve this generic noun for prose where enrolment itself, not the person, is the point.

scenario.task: Write a 120-word entry for an in-house style guide explaining what the word student actually means to a reader, why writers reach for it, and what it does to a sentence.

draft: This little adjective is the widest praise term in English: it fits any subject, and by itself it tells the reader very little. Writers reach here in a first draft, while the true detail is still missing. An item might be quick, tidy, cheap, careful, sturdy, kind - each a real claim, each testable - and a first draft picks this single lazy term instead. In a print sentence it can even dilute what it prizes: a fine meal, a fine year, a fine argument, all levelled by the same three letters. In client writing it invites a fair challenge: what element, precisely, made it that? Strike it in edits unless the sentence can name that element.

scenario.task: Write a 120-word entry for an in-house style guide explaining what the word good actually means to a reader, why writers reach for it, and what it does to a sentence.

draft: This noun points to the people who show, correct, drill, comfort, plus enforce: one job, six or seven very different roles. Writers pick it since it is short, since it is respectful, since it seems to cover the whole institution. In its sentence it tends to blur people who hold little in common: the just-hired, the deputy who runs thirty other people, the supply cover in her fifth week, the union rep, the one months from retirement. Prefer the precise role where you know it: the deputy, the tutor, the visiting instructor, the mentor. Give this noun its job only where the profession itself, not one person, is the subject.

scenario.task: Write a 120-word entry for an in-house style guide explaining what the word teachers actually means to a reader, why writers reach for it, and what it does to a sentence.

draft: Copywriters pick this word for one motive: it puts effort, length, plus suffering into one term, so nobody needs telling how long the thing is. It shows up in every pitch for HR resilience, for products which promise stubbornness, for projects with brutish timelines. It mostly does duty for four different notions: it is long; it will hurt; nobody wins it in one shot; you must prep for months. Which of those four do you intend? Push it into the sentence itself. This borrowed figure is so common now it is close to invisible, so the simple, unborrowed line under it still does the job better.

scenario.task: Explain to a room of new copywriters why the word marathon keeps turning up in first drafts, and what it usually stands in for.

draft: Most folks still spot this word and think of a black box on a strap, with a big glass ring at its front, ticking and whirring. That kit is now a minority. In daily fact most of this work is digital, in a slim slab you also call folks on, in a small flying rig, in a car door, in a shop's alarm layout, in a lab that maps an anthill in full dark. Is that first instinct wrong? Not fully. Any kit that pulls light in and stamps a still or a clip will fit this word, and a strap-and-glass unit was our first form of it, so folks link word and form justly, if too narrowly.

scenario.task: Draft a 100-word paragraph for a plain-language guide about the word camera, covering what readers assume when they meet it and whether that assumption is fair.

draft: Roots first: this word is old, a Nordic and Gothic word for a soft mass you push, fold, and turn, and it has sat in our own word stock for a thousand-odd springs without much drift. Its craft-hall job is still its main slot: flour, salt, liquid, and a lot of thumb work. It is also cash, a slang from about 1850, which is why it pops up in tabloid froth about rich folk. That is what most writing folk fight about. To many a copy pro it is warm and solid; to a stylist watching a paragraph tilt into slang, it is a wink you would want to cut.

scenario.task: Write a short piece for a language column on the word dough: its history, its current sense, and the reason editors argue about it.

draft: Readers meet the term and picture three things: a sunlit hillside, a family name at the gate, and a life ruled by the calendar rather than the till. The reality is a farm, and a fussy plant. The year runs early starts, mildew watch, trellis repairs, spray timings, and a frantic week when the pickers arrive and the entire year is settled in three days. A late April freeze can erase twelve preceding treatments. Is the reader's picture fair? Nearly. The site really is family-held, gently timed, and pretty; it is likewise a business with debt, chemistry, and a single yearly payday.

scenario.task: Draft a 100-word paragraph for a plain-language guide about the word vineyard, covering what readers assume when they meet it and whether that assumption is fair.

draft: This word is young: it took its form from a Latin root for a footing or floor, plus a tail that turns things into an -ly word, and it took off, as a stall word, only in our own day. In talk it works as a warning light: what follows will skip a lot of small print. In writing that job is mostly null. Drop it and no part of your point falls out. So why do word folk fight? A small camp will back it as a fair flag on a simplification. A vast majority find it a stall, put in for rhythm, saying nothing at all.

scenario.task: Write a short piece for a language column on the word basically: its history, its current sense, and the reason editors argue about it.

draft: This word is a stand-in for cold, long-run plotting. Its origin is Indo-Iranian, from a word for a king, and it got to us through Latin and Old Spanish. In most copy it is not about a light-and-dark grid at all: it is a claim about a rival two turns forward, about traps laid four turns out, about a calm brain doing a long calculation. What it puts into a paragraph is a cool, cunning tint, plus a lot of unsaid glory for that party. So sit on it. It is glamour, not information, and a rival's plotting will look sharp only until you spill out its actual parts.

scenario.task: Write a 120-word entry for an in-house style guide explaining what the word chess actually means to a reader, why writers reach for it, and what it does to a sentence.

draft: It arrives early in any brief with a bakery in it, and it arrives in the cash lines as well, which is exactly why it is a slippery pick. In craft writing it means warmth, patience, the hand in the mix; it hints at 5am, at yeast, at heat, at a family trade. In cash writing it means easy, unearned wealth, and it carries a wink with it. A writer will reach here when they want the reader in a warm kitchen and never in a plant with steel trays. Name what the mix really is: rye, wheat, salt, water, and the sheer patience it takes.

scenario.task: Explain to a room of new copywriters why the word dough keeps turning up in first drafts, and what it usually stands in for.

draft: Readers meet this word and picture a person in a white coat with a stethoscope, but the word is doing three jobs at once. It is a job title, earned by a specific licence. It is an academic rank, held by historians and chemists who never see a ward. And it is a social signal: expertise, seniority, the right to be believed. Most readers assume the first sense, which is fair in a health story and unfair in a research one, where the person may hold a doctorate in economics. If the sense matters to your sentence, name the field or the licence and let the reader stop guessing.

scenario.task: Draft a 100-word paragraph for a plain-language guide about the word doctor, covering what readers assume when they meet it and whether that assumption is fair.

draft: The term grew from one root, sign: to possess this property once implied showing something, pointing to it, while the rest of the world just sits there. Since then two senses split off. The common one is loose - big enough to notice, worth your time. The strict one belongs to figure-work: it points to results unlikely to be flukes. Those two collide in prose, since one uses the other's credit. It sits wrong most obviously in copy where the writer holds no number, no test, no shred of proof, yet the word implies every one of them. Prefer the simple, defensible size term: bigger, quicker, or nine per cent less costly.

scenario.task: A dictionary editor has asked for a short entry describing the word significant: where it came from, how it is handled today, and one sentence on the writing where it feels out of place.

draft: The term began life with a concrete meaning: in the older Germanic tongue it named a public council, an open-air court, an appointed meeting. By the medieval period it had drifted along a common path: a matter met about, then a matter, then any matter, and at length any object, act, or notion at all. Today it will name nearly the entire world, and that width invited a century-long quarrel. One camp deleted it wherever they met it, on the ground that it named nothing. Another camp let it live, calling it the hinge on which the entire tongue can turn.

scenario.task: Write a short piece for a language column on the word thing: its history, its current sense, and the reason editors argue about it.

draft: This noun now covers two very different objects: the file your phone put there without thinking, plus the print somebody hung, lit, licensed, then insured. Writers use it since it is short, since it offends nobody, since it fits every context. It fits so well it hides your costs: whose shots? Which licence, running how long, over which region? In our copy prefer the specific term - the studio shot, the phone still, the press print, the screenshot, the drone flyover - so the sentence tells the truth or else tells the client which one they must license before shipping.

scenario.task: Write a 120-word entry for an in-house style guide explaining what the word photos actually means to a reader, why writers reach for it, and what it does to a sentence.

draft: Folks run into this word and think a ranking is at work: this bit sits up top, and all following bits sit low. That thought is only half right. A ranking word works only if a low rank turns up too. Pull it out of any policy handbook and count: if all six points claim top billing, no ranking was truly said at all. So a fair way to skim: hunt for a why, a cost, or a proof standing right by it. If nothing backs it up, our word is just a spotlight our author aims at his own point, and you can walk right past it.

scenario.task: Draft a 100-word paragraph for a plain-language guide about the word important, covering what readers assume when they meet it and whether that assumption is fair.

draft: Readers meet that three-word opener and take two notes at once: a computer, not a human, made the text, and a hedge probably follows. The second note reads as an excuse - the wall a model puts up when the ask goes past what the maker allows. Both hold true often enough that readers now skate over the clause and hunt for the refusal underneath. That makes the phrase dull rather than honest. One more note: the clause sets up a two-part shape, a hedge and then a moderate answer, and readers have learnt to expect the second part to matter less than the fuss. Better to name the true cause up front: no such record was found, no answer was safe to release, or the request broke a rule the reader never knew about.

scenario.task: Draft a 100-word paragraph for a plain-language guide about the phrase as an ai, covering what readers assume when they meet it and whether that assumption is fair.

draft: Most readers meet the word and picture a quiet room, long tables, and shelves that go up to the ceiling. That picture is about a third of the truth. A modern branch lends power tools and instruments, runs the only free warm room in the district, hosts baby groups and job clubs, and puts a trained person between a frightened claimant and a benefits form. The reading collection is still the heart of it, but the assumption that reading is all of it explains why funders keep cutting them: you cannot defend a service if you only understand a third of what it does.

scenario.task: Draft a 100-word paragraph for a plain-language guide about the word libraries, covering what readers assume when they meet it and whether that assumption is fair.

draft: The term will land in nearly every brief about method, and it will land there for one clear motive: it can pledge an outcome without pledging the labour. What the term will actually cover: a method, an order, a timing, and one named yield. It will carry a kitchen aroma with it - warmth, family, a hand-written card in a tin - which no other method word can carry. Where the term can trick your reader: no unit, no interval, no temperature, and a claim that anyone at all can repeat the outcome. Before you print the term, count what you can really put in the method: each ingredient, each interval, each yield.

scenario.task: Explain to a room of new copywriters why the word recipe keeps turning up in first drafts, and what it usually stands in for.

draft: The plural noun is one of the oldest in English, older than most of the vocabulary around it, and it has barely shifted shape in a thousand years: sung verse, words fitted to a tune. What has shifted is what it points at. Once it named a performance, something a person did in a room; then it named a printed sheet you bought; then a recording; now, most often, a file with a play count next to it. Editors argue about the edges. Is a sixty-second clip built for a phone app one of them? Is an instrumental track? The word keeps the argument alive because it was never a technical term, only a human one.

scenario.task: Write a short piece for a language column on the word songs: its history, its current sense, and the reason editors argue about it.

draft: This noun does three very different jobs in English, so context, not the noun, does the work here. First, the group who perform together: three or four folk, one set list, one drummer with hopes. Second, the strip which ties, seizes or trims: rubber, iron, wedding gold. Third, the tier: the income group, the top or bottom bit of some numbered set. Writers pick it since it is short, since it is common, since it fits every register. Its cost is comic misfires: our copy on high income tiers should not conjure four youths with one drum kit. One sense per sentence, or rewrite the sentence.

scenario.task: Write a 120-word entry for an in-house style guide explaining what the word band actually means to a reader, why writers reach for it, and what it does to a sentence.

draft: The term will move nearly every reader to picture the identical creature: fat, warm, wobbly on a kitchen tile, one ear too big for the head. That picture will be real for a little while, and then it will not. What the term never carried: the 4am walk in the rain, the chewed cable, the bitten thumb, the vet bill in month one, the fourteen-year commitment made in an afternoon. Fair? Partly. The warmth and the comedy really did arrive with the little animal, and no term can carry the whole truth. Anyone who bought one on the term alone met the other half by week three.

scenario.task: Draft a 100-word paragraph for a plain-language guide about the word puppies, covering what readers assume when they meet it and whether that assumption is fair.

draft: The plural noun names a group by what was done to them, not by who they are, and that is the whole of the problem with it. Writers reach for it because the health system runs on it: the ward list, the waiting figure, the outcome data. It is efficient and it is cold. In a sentence it turns individuals into a countable mass, which is exactly right in a statistics paragraph and exactly wrong in a story about one person having a bad night. House rule: use the clinical plural for populations and numbers. When a single human being is the subject, use their name, or the people we care for, and let them keep their grammar as a subject rather than an object.

scenario.task: Write a 120-word entry for an in-house style guide explaining what the word patients actually means to a reader, why writers reach for it, and what it does to a sentence.

draft: It turns up in first drafts because it is the fastest way to tell a reader this matters without explaining why it matters. Nine times in ten it is a placeholder for a number the writer has not looked up yet: how much bigger, how much faster, how many people affected. It also carries a borrowed authority from statistics, where it has a strict technical sense, and copy quietly cashes in on that borrowed rigour without doing any of the work. Two fixes. Give the figure, or give the consequence: what happens to the reader if they ignore this. Either one beats the adjective, and both are harder to argue with.

scenario.task: Explain to a room of new copywriters why the word significant keeps turning up in first drafts, and what it usually stands in for.

draft: The term came the long way round: from a Latin word for a cooking pot, then through the older northern tongue, where it meant a deep metal container held over a fire. That older meaning covered nearly any big metal container above a flame, and the narrowed meaning we carry now, a container for hot water alone, arrived quite late. In Britain the term will mean an electric jug on the counter; in America it can mean the burner-top kind, hooting at the cook. That divide will feed the whole argument: one camp will keep the term tied to metal over a flame, another will let the plug-in jug carry it. A word can outlive the metal it named, and that lag will hold for a decade or two.

scenario.task: Write a short piece for a language column on the word kettle: its history, its current sense, and the reason editors argue about it.

draft: The word does two jobs at once. One names a character on a page, the smallest part of a word, one of the twenty-odd parts that make up the alphabet. The other names a note sent from one person to another, folded, stamped, dropped through a door. Readers sort the two apart from context alone, and rarely stumble. We reach for the short, common word because the exact term for each sense feels overblown, and because both senses grew from the same old root. Add a noun next to the word wherever a page could go two ways: a bold character, a sealed note, a stamped envelope.

scenario.task: Write a 120-word entry for an in-house style guide explaining what the word letter actually means to a reader, why writers reach for it, and what it does to a sentence.

draft: Readers meet the word and assume paper: a bound block of pages, printed, sold in a shop, kept on a shelf. That assumption is fair for most of the last five centuries and steadily less fair now. The same word covers an audio file read aloud by an actor, a licensed download that vanishes when a service closes, a serialised text delivered in an app one chapter at a time. What survives across all of those is not paper at all: it is a single long work by a named author, edited, finished, and released as one thing. Keep the word for that, and say paperback or file when the physical form is what actually matters.

scenario.task: Draft a 100-word paragraph for a plain-language guide about the word book, covering what readers assume when they meet it and whether that assumption is fair.

draft: The word came from sang, an Anglo-Saxon noun bound to the verb for what a throat does to a tune. That form goes back a long way. Today the term covers three cases at once: the sung form on a page, the record made from the same, and the loose trade product a label sells to us. Two of those are recent. Where the term sounds odd: at a funeral, where a modern speaker announces a hymn as a number, and the crowd hears a chart term where a sacred one was meant. Compare that to a broadcast, where announcers say the same word all day and the crowd never blanches at all.

scenario.task: A dictionary editor has asked for a short entry describing the word song: where it came from, how it is handled today, and one sentence on the writing where it feels out of place.

draft: It turns up in first drafts because it is a fast way to say a large, vague thing: young, learning, not yet expert, probably broke. Half the time the copy is not about education at all. A gym uses it to mean under twenty-five with a card. A landlord uses it to mean a tenant who will accept a bad room. A software company uses it to mean the cheap tier of a licence. Ask which of those you mean and write that instead: under twenty-five, first-year trainee, the discounted tier. The line gets shorter, the claim gets checkable, and nobody has to guess which of the four senses you had in mind.

scenario.task: Explain to a room of new copywriters why the word student keeps turning up in first drafts, and what it usually stands in for.

draft: The term comes down from liber, the tender flesh under the tree's outer skin, which held some very old writing. Then the term went to the room which held the loot. Then to this civic institution: doors open to entry, no fee, no test of worth. Presently the print is just one item on one long list: printers, kits, hot rooms in November, meeting rooms, wifi, plus the one person who helps others with the benefit form. This is why some editors dispute the term. Some hold it pulls the mind onto the print, so the term hides most of the true work. Others defend it, since the money follows the loved term, not the fully truthful term.

scenario.task: Write a short piece for a language column on the word libraries: its history, its current sense, and the reason editors argue about it.

draft: The plural noun names the moment a program stops without being asked to, and it carries a whole story in seven letters: something broke, a user lost work, and nobody chose it. Writers reach for it because it is vivid and short, and because the alternative, unplanned termination of the process, sounds like a coroner talking. What it does to a sentence is smuggle in blame. It implies suddenness and violence, which flatters a support team when the truth is a slow memory leak, and it flatters nobody when the real cause was a config change signed off last Tuesday. House style: use the noun in incident titles and user-facing notes, where speed of reading wins. In the write-up, name the failure mode instead.

scenario.task: Write a 120-word entry for an in-house style guide explaining what the word crashes actually means to a reader, why writers reach for it, and what it does to a sentence.

draft: This word sat first on a thin skin: a coating, a fog of dust on glass, a wash of oil across a pond. Photography took it for a strip of stock with just such a coating, and by 1900 that strip stood in for all of a night's outing at a hall. Now no strip is in it at all: digital data, a card, a hard disk, and a bright lamp in a box at a hall's back. That is what critics fight about. A small group of purists want a strip and a hot lamp or nothing at all; a vast group point at a ship's log, which is digital now and still a log.

scenario.task: Write a short piece for a language column on the word films: its history, its current sense, and the reason editors argue about it.

draft: This letter is the ring: the shape the pen makes in a single sweep, and the lips make that very same ring when it speaks. In the middle in a brief, shut syllable - the three-letter name we give a cat's rival, the tin bell's clang, the little mark a pen leaves at a sentence's tail - the jaw hangs slack, the lips barely gather, and the utterance is brief and dull. At the tail end it will nearly always sing its alphabet name in full: the greeting we give at the gate, the number that is nil, the call the cliffs send back at us, the black-and-white keyed instrument in the hall. English will rarely leave that brief kind bare at the tail; the final place stretches it. Try the pair with the class, in the middle and then at the tail, and their ears will catch the shift.

scenario.task: Explain to a class of nine-year-olds what the letter o sounds like in ordinary speech and why it behaves differently at the end of a word.

draft: Readers meet the word and assume the raw stage: flour, water, yeast, a lump under a cloth in a warm corner, waiting to be worked. That assumption is fair as far as it goes, and it goes about half way. The same word does two other jobs. It is money, in casual speech, from a chain of slang that runs back to the eighteen-hundreds. And it is a texture: anything soft, pale and yielding gets called it, from a pale forearm to a weak argument. The raw-stage sense is the oldest and the safest bet, so a reader who lands there first is landing sensibly, and the other two announce themselves by context.

scenario.task: Draft a 100-word paragraph for a plain-language guide about the word dough, covering what readers assume when they meet it and whether that assumption is fair.

draft: Readers meet the word and picture one thing: a person at the front of a classroom, holding chalk. That picture is fair for the largest group who hold the job, and it quietly excludes most of the others. The same word covers the driving instructor, the swimming coach, the apprentice supervisor on a building site, the parent at the kitchen table with a phonics card, and the person who trains adults to use a new payroll system. It also carries a set of assumptions the job itself does not: female, underpaid, endlessly patient, vaguely saintly. Both the narrow picture and the halo do the profession a quiet disservice, because neither leaves room for a person who is simply good at a difficult, technical job.

scenario.task: Draft a 100-word paragraph for a plain-language guide about the word teacher, covering what readers assume when they meet it and whether that assumption is fair.

draft: The reader meets the term and pictures three minutes: a verse, a repeated part that returns, and a singer at the centre. That guess is fair in the main, since the entire industry has been built near that shape and that length. It is unfair at the edges. It leaves the hymn, the chant, the lullaby, the nine-minute epic, and every sung piece with never a lyric in it, all sitting just at the rim; a listener will still stretch the term wide there. Where the tighter meaning matters is in a licence, a bill, a legal deal, since the term underpins the fee that changes hands per unit.

scenario.task: Draft a 100-word paragraph for a plain-language guide about the word songs, covering what readers assume when they meet it and whether that assumption is fair.

draft: The term carries three different senses, and a careless sentence will let them slip. First, the plan: a spreadsheet, with entries by team and by quarter. Then the ceiling: the cash any given team may spend at all. Then the adjective, filed under cheap: the seat with the least knee space, the cheaper cabin, the thin end. Writers reach here since it feels neutral, technical, settled, as if the figure were a fact rather than a call which a named human made. That is exactly its risk in a sentence: it can bury whichever team set the limit. Internal rule: name the sense, and if the ceiling is meant, name whichever team put it there.

scenario.task: Write a 120-word entry for an in-house style guide explaining what the word budget actually means to a reader, why writers reach for it, and what it does to a sentence.

draft: This noun covers one duty: the person up front, holding the room, checking the effort of everyone else in the room. Writers pick it since everyone knows it, since it is short, since it sounds respectful without being stuffy. Its one limit is precision. In writing on schools it will hide the tiers under it: the newly enrolled novice, the deputy shepherding thirty other people, the union rep, the supply cover, the tutor who sees sixty different pupils per week. House rule: keep this noun for the profession itself, not the specific job, plus put the precise title in where you know it.

draft: It turns up early in first drafts because it sounds like a benefit and costs nothing to claim. Nine times in ten it is standing in for one of four much duller nouns. Sometimes it means a discount: this price is lower than that price, once. Sometimes it means avoided spend: work you now will not have to pay for. Sometimes it means time, converted to cash at a rate nobody in the room agreed. And sometimes it means a projection, which is a hope in a suit. Ask which of the four you mean, then write the number and the period it covers. A claim with a number attached survives legal review; the vague noun does not.

scenario.task: Explain to a room of new copywriters why the word savings keeps turning up in first drafts, and what it usually stands in for.

draft: The word is one of the oldest oddities in English: it appears around 1300 with no clear parent, unlike almost every other core adjective in the language, and etymologists still argue over whether it came from an Old English word for an effeminate man or from somewhere lost entirely. Today it does an enormous amount of work, from moral judgement to spoiled milk to a leg that hurts, and it has picked up an inverted slang sense that means the opposite. It sits oddly in technical writing, where a reviewer who calls a proposal weak is understood, while the shorter word reads as a verdict on the author rather than the work.

scenario.task: A dictionary editor has asked for a short entry describing the word bad: where it came from, how it is handled today, and one sentence on the writing where it feels out of place.

draft: The plural noun comes into English from an Old French word for a leather pouch, the little bag a man carried his coins in. The pouch sense died; the sense of what is in the pouch survived, and by the eighteenth century a chancellor was opening his to announce the year's finances. That is where the modern sense comes from, and the metaphor still shows in the language around it: it is opened, it is stretched, it is tight, it runs out. It is handled today as a plural of plans rather than of pouches, which is why a sentence can speak of three departmental ones without anybody hearing leather. It reads oddly in a family setting, where the word imports a boardroom into a conversation about groceries.

scenario.task: A dictionary editor has asked for a short entry describing the word budgets: where it came from, how it is handled today, and one sentence on the writing where it feels out of place.

draft: The word comes from a verb that meant to show or to point out, which is why the oldest sense is closer to demonstrating than to explaining. The agent suffix does the rest of the work: one who shows. It is handled today as the neutral, official term for the whole profession, the one that appears in pay scales, union names and legislation, while the warmer alternatives are reserved for particular settings: tutor for one-to-one work, lecturer for universities, instructor for practical skills, coach for sport. It sits awkwardly in adult training, where the person on the receiving end resents the schoolroom echo, and where facilitator, a word almost nobody likes, survives largely because the older word carries too much childhood with it.

scenario.task: A dictionary editor has asked for a short entry describing the word teacher: where it came from, how it is handled today, and one sentence on the writing where it feels out of place.

draft: It keeps turning up because it is the most respectable-sounding word for the thing everybody in the room is actually thinking about, which is money and who controls it. In a first draft it almost always stands in for something more specific and more awkward. Often it means a ceiling: the point past which the client will say no. Sometimes it means a plan already signed, which is a very different thing from a hope. Sometimes it means the finance team, personified, as in that will not survive them. And sometimes it is pure hedging, a way of raising price without saying price. Work out which one you mean, then say it plainly: the cap is forty thousand, the approval sits with finance, the plan is signed until March.

draft: The term came intact out of the older Germanic tongue, kin to nearly every neighbouring word for it: nix, neige, nieve, all born of one ancient root, and hardly altered in a millennium. Today it can mean the fall, the layer left behind, the verb for what the cloud did, or the flicker on an old dead TV. The quarrel: a familiar claim that one northern tongue had a hundredfold vocabulary for it. It never did, not in that count, and the correction never quite caught up with the tale. The quarrel did leave one valuable lever behind: a tongue will grow the vocabulary the daily life of the folk near it demand, and not one term more.

scenario.task: Write a short piece for a language column on the word snow: its history, its current sense, and the reason editors argue about it.

draft: The noun names element number six, the backbone of every organic molecule, and in most copy it means none of that. It has become a shorthand for greenhouse emissions, which is why a company can announce it is removing it from the atmosphere without anyone asking which compound, at what concentration, or for how long. Writers reach for it because it is short, scientific-sounding and uncontroversial, and because the honest phrase, tonnes of dioxide equivalent per year, is a mouthful nobody wants in a headline. In a sentence it lets a vague promise wear a lab coat. House rule: name the gas, the mass and the deadline, or write the plain verb instead: we will burn less gas by 2030.
